newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico stocks edge up on year-end portfolio close.
newsitem.headline: Mexico stocks edge up on year-end portfolio close.

text.p: MEXICO CITY - Mexican stocks held on to earlier gains at the close on Monday despite a slump in the Wall Street as brokers bought stocks prior to closing their portfolios for the year.
"A very boring session, as you can see from the volume. Just a little buying to close portfolios for the year tipped the scales," a trader said.
The blue chip IPC index closed up 19.75 points, or 0.59 percent, at 3,346.95. Volume was a moribund 23.8 million shares.
Stocks had been at a virtual standstill since chalking up most of their gains in early trade on an advance by market heavyweight Telmex, which closed up 18 centavos (2 cents) at 12.90 pesos ($1.64).
Traders noted that Mexican stocks closed up despite the Dow Jones closing off 11.54 points, or 0.18 percent, at 6.549.37 points.
"Volume was so thin today the Dow had no effect one way or the other. Besides, foreign dealers were totally absent," a dealer said.

Traders also dismissed expected primary rate falls as a factor in gains in share prices. Traders expected bellwether 28-day Cetes (Treasury bill) rates to fall 0.69 percentage points to 26.56 percent.
On the broad market, a total of 102 stocks changed hands, of which gainers outnumbered losers by 55 to 27.
Traders pointed to the predominance of infrequently traded stocks at the head of the gainers' list, at thin-volume trades, due to last-minute portfolio adjustments.

Hotel operator Posadas headed the gains, up 46 centavos (6 cents) at 3.56 pesos (45 cents). Holding company Sidek was in fourth place, up five centavos (1 cent) at one peso (13 cents), on expectations of a plan to restructure its substantial debt burden, traders said.
Most-heavily traded slider was financial stock GFCrece, off 13 centavos (2 cents) at 1.17 pesos (15 cents).
Financial stocks in general were trading poorly due to the impending introduction of accountancy practices closer to international guidelines, traders said.
The new criteria, they said, would increase balance-sheet estimates of past-due loans and thus force banks to create more reserves.
